bull_thesis: The bull case is that the activist campaign eventually forces a sale of the whole company, and that the leverage on the balance sheet turns a modest move in the takeover multiple into a very large move in the share price. Six Flags Entertainment, which trades under the ticker FUN because the surviving entity of the July 2024 merger is the old Cedar Fair vehicle, runs regional amusement parks across North America. JANA Partners, an activist investment firm, disclosed an economic interest of about 9% on 21 October 2025 alongside Travis Kelce, former Gap and Lululemon chief executive Glenn Murphy, and technology executive Dave Habiger, and on 17 March 2026 publicly demanded the board explore an outright sale and replace its chair. That campaign is still live and has not been withdrawn. The board has already conceded a great deal: a new chief executive (John Reilly, announced 24 November 2025), an executive chairman brought in on 25 March 2026 (Richard Haddrill), a cooperation agreement with a second activist, H Partners, on 19 May 2026 that seated Rehan Jaffer on the board after the 26 May 2026 annual meeting, a new chief financial officer on 17 June 2026 and a new chief operating officer on 15 July 2026. Boards that concede governance this quickly sometimes concede the company a year later. The arithmetic is what makes the bull case worth stating at all. At $17.59 a share the equity is worth about $1.80B while enterprise value is about $7.21B, because net debt was $5.42B at 29 March 2026. The equity is therefore a thin slice on top of a very large debt load, and it is extremely sensitive to the multiple applied to earnings. On roughly $820M of full-year 2026 adjusted profit before interest, tax, depreciation and amortisation, a buyer paying about ten and a half times - a normal price for irreplaceable regional park land - produces roughly $31 a share, or about 75% above the current price. That is where the board entry's $31 target comes from. There is an operating leg too. The first quarter of 2026 was genuinely better: revenue up 12% to $225.6M, attendance up 4% to 2.9 million visits, spending per visitor up 6% to $69.26, and the seasonal loss narrowed by $48M to a $123M adjusted loss before interest, tax, depreciation and amortisation. Management has said openly that the 27% margin earned in 2025 is not good enough against regional peers in the low thirties. If the new team closes even half that gap, the same multiple on higher earnings gets to a similar place without any sale at all. The seven-park disposal to EPR Properties for $331.4M in cash, agreed 4 March 2026 and closed in April for the US parks, shows the board will monetise assets under pressure. Conditions this case depends on: a credible buyer must actually appear and finance a deal with an enterprise value above seven billion dollars; the board must be willing to transact near ten and a half times rather than hold out; attendance must stabilise so that the earnings base being multiplied is real; and the quarterly net first-lien leverage covenant must not be tripped in the meantime.
bear_thesis: The bear case is that there is no sale, no date, and no floor - and that the same leverage which powers the bull case destroys the equity on the way down. Start with the event. Nothing about it is dated or binding. The 2026 annual meeting was held on 26 May 2026 and no activist slate went to a vote, so the proxy window that could have forced the issue this year has closed; the next natural pressure point is the nomination window for the 2027 meeting, which has no announced date. JANA's own release of 24 November 2025 disclosed that Glenn Murphy had de-grouped from the investor group to discuss a senior leadership role with the board and that Dave Habiger remained de-grouped to pursue a separate opportunity involving the company - two of three named operating partners absorbed into the target within weeks. The board seat that did change hands went to a different activist, H Partners, under the 19 May 2026 cooperation agreement. Every demand for a sale has been answered with something cheaper and adjacent: a chair, a director seat for someone else, seven peripheral parks. No sale process, strategic review or data room has been announced in any filing through 28 July 2026. Now the floor, which is the part of the board entry that does not survive contact with the tape. The entry assumes a downside floor of $16.50 against a live price of $17.59 - about 6% of risk. The shares traded at $12.51 within the last twelve months, 29% below that level. A price the security has recently traded straight through is not a floor. There is no asset backstop underneath it either. At 29 March 2026 the company held $116.5M of cash against $5.53B of total debt, $5.42B net, with $235M of minority interest ahead of common holders and total shareholders' equity down to $279M after a $1.19B net loss in the third quarter of 2025 (a loss of $11.80 a share) that wrote off merger goodwill. Retained earnings stand at negative $2.03B. Free cash flow is close to nothing: capital spending absorbed about 93% of operating cash flow over the trailing twelve months, leaving about $29M of trailing free cash flow against interest expense running near $95M a quarter. The company cannot deleverage out of cash flow; it can only sell assets. Because the equity is a thin slice of a $7.21B enterprise, one turn of multiple compression is worth roughly $10 a share. Eight and a half times $800M of earnings is about $15 a share; seven and a half times $760M is about $7. And the relevant market-clearing comparable points the wrong way: EPR Properties paid roughly eight and a half times for the seven-park package, well below the ten and a half times the $31 target requires. The near-term news flow is already confirming the bear case. On 19 July 2026 Citi cut its price target from $24 to $19 with a neutral rating and Guggenheim also cut, both citing softer attendance, with hazardous air quality from Ontario wildfires affecting fourteen parks across the Upper Midwest and Great Lakes during the peak season. Jefferies carries a below-consensus full-year 2026 estimate of about $865M and warns street attendance assumptions are too high. What would confirm the bear case: a weak second-quarter print on 6 August 2026; a third quarter that captures the July weather damage; any commentary that pushes the quarterly net first-lien leverage test toward its limit; and the passing of the 2027 nomination window without a slate.
sop_bull: Event-win value: about $30 to $31 a share. Derivation: a whole-company sale at roughly ten and a half times full-year adjusted profit before interest, tax, depreciation and amortisation of about $850M gives an enterprise value near $8.9B; subtract about $5.15B of expected year-end 2026 net debt (net debt was $5.42B at the seasonal peak on 29 March 2026, less the $331.4M of EPR proceeds received in April) and $235M of minority interest, leaving roughly $3.1B of equity across about 101.5 million shares. Ten and a half times is defensible for irreplaceable regional park land - Cedar Point, Knott's Berry Farm, Magic Mountain - in a financial buyer's hands, and it is the multiple implied by the board entry's own $31 target. A self-help path reaches a similar place more slowly: if the margin gap management has acknowledged (27% in 2025 against regional peers above 30%) is half closed, roughly $900M of earnings at nine and a half times is about $32 a share.
sop_bear: Verified downside floor: about $10 to $12 a share, not the $16.50 the board entry assumes. Derivation, three independent ways. First, the tape: the 52-week low is $12.51, set within the past twelve months, which is a level the market has already been willing to pay - and there is nothing structural beneath it. Second, the multiple: at eight and a half times - the rough multiple EPR Properties paid for the seven-park package in the only recent arm's-length transaction in these assets - on about $800M of earnings, enterprise value is $6.8B, which after $5.15B of net debt and $235M of minority interest leaves about $1.4B of equity, or roughly $14 a share; at seven and a half times on $760M it is about $7. Third, the balance sheet offers no backstop at all: $116.5M of cash, $5.53B of total debt, $279M of book equity, negative $2.03B of retained earnings, tangible asset value of negative $2.24B, and trailing free cash flow of roughly $29M against interest expense near $380M a year. In an outright attendance recession that trips the quarterly net first-lien leverage covenant, the equity is worth materially less than $7. The honest statement is that this equity has no verified floor - $10 to $12 is a judgement about where forced sellers stopped last time, not a backstop.
sop_breakdown: Base case of about $18 a share, which is a probability-weighted blend rather than a single valuation, because a levered equity stub does not have a central case so much as a barbell. Weighting: roughly 20% chance of a whole-company sale at about ten and a half times earnings, worth about $30; roughly 40% chance the turnaround works without a sale and the market pays about nine and a quarter times a higher earnings base, worth about $22; roughly 40% chance attendance keeps sliding and the multiple compresses toward eight times or below, worth about $9. That blend is $18.60, which is within a dollar of the live price of $17.59. The parts, for orientation: enterprise value at the current price is about $7.21B, of which the operating park portfolio after the seven-park disposal is essentially all of it. Against that sit $5.42B of net debt at the 29 March 2026 seasonal peak (roughly $5.15B expected at year end after $331.4M of EPR proceeds received in April), $235M of minority interest, and $116.5M of cash. Common equity is the residual across about 101.5 million shares. Because debt is roughly three quarters of enterprise value, each single turn of multiple on about $820M of earnings is worth roughly $8 to $10 a share to the equity - which is why the honest fair value is a range spanning more than three times from bottom to top, and why the mean sits almost exactly on the market price. There is no measurable edge in this valuation.
risk_reward: Roughly 1.6 to 1 gross, and negative once probability is applied - not the 2.6 to 1 the board entry claims. Upside to the event-resolved target of about $30 is roughly +71% from $17.59. Downside to the verified floor of about $10 to $12 is roughly -32% to -43%. The board entry's 2.6 to 1 depended entirely on a $16.50 floor implying only 6% of risk, and that floor was broken by the market at $12.51 within the past twelve months. Adjusting for odds makes it worse: the sale outcome carries perhaps a one-in-five chance with no date and no identified buyer, while the downside scenarios are being actively confirmed by July attendance news and two broker target cuts. The expected value sits at or slightly below the current price.
catalyst_summary: An undated, non-binding activist push by JANA Partners (about 9% economic interest, sale demand letter 17 March 2026) that the board has so far answered with governance changes and asset sales rather than a sale process; the 2026 proxy window closed at the 26 May 2026 annual meeting without a contested vote, and the claimed $16.50 downside floor was already broken at $12.51 within the past year, so the asymmetry is roughly +71% against -35% rather than the 6%-risk trade it was written up as.
dated_milestone: No dated milestone attaches to the catalyst itself. The only firm dates on the calendar are operating, not event, dates: second-quarter 2026 results before the open on Thursday 6 August 2026 with a call at 8am Eastern, and the quarterly net first-lien leverage covenant test under the 2024 credit agreement at each quarter end. The activist forcing points that have already passed are the 26 May 2026 annual meeting (held with no contested vote) and the 19 May 2026 cooperation agreement with H Partners. The next potential forcing point is the director nomination window for the 2027 annual meeting, which has not been announced and sits roughly six to nine months ahead.
forcing_function: There is no genuine forcing function in place today, and that is the central finding. What would have forced a re-rating - a contested vote at the 26 May 2026 annual meeting - did not happen; JANA ran no slate, and the board seat that changed hands went to a different activist, H Partners' Rehan Jaffer, under a cooperation agreement signed 19 May 2026. Two of the three operating partners JANA named in its October 2025 group had already de-grouped by 24 November 2025 to pursue roles with the company. Three things could become forcing functions, in descending order of likelihood. First, and nearest, second-quarter results on 6 August 2026 - but that is an earnings print, and the evidence points to it being a risk rather than a catalyst, given Citi's 19 July 2026 cut from $24 to $19 and Guggenheim's cut, both on soft attendance including wildfire smoke advisories across fourteen parks. Second, further asset sales in the pattern of the $331.4M EPR Properties disposal, which deleverage but also shrink the earnings base being multiplied. Third, the 2027 director nomination window, which would let JANA actually run the slate it threatened - unannounced, and roughly six to nine months away. A whole-company sale remains possible but has no date, no announced process, and no identified buyer, and would require financing an enterprise value above seven billion dollars.
consensus_delta: The disagreement here is not with Wall Street's view of the business - it is with our own board entry's view of the risk. The street is, if anything, roughly right: Citi cut to $19 with a neutral rating on 19 July 2026, Guggenheim cut on softer attendance while keeping a $28 target, and Jefferies sits below consensus at about $865M of full-year 2026 earnings before interest, tax, depreciation and amortisation, warning that street attendance and revenue assumptions are too optimistic. The shares at $17.59 sit between the bear and bull marks. That is a market doing its job. Where we disagree with the write-up that brought this name to the committee is on two specific claims. The first is that the downside is bounded at $16.50. It is not - the shares printed $12.51 within the last twelve months, and the balance sheet offers nothing beneath that: $116.5M of cash against $5.53B of total debt, book equity of $279M, tangible asset value of negative $2.24B, and trailing free cash flow near $29M. The second is that the activist process is a live catalyst. On the evidence it has been managed rather than obeyed: the sale demand of 17 March 2026 was answered with an executive chairman on 25 March, a cooperation agreement with a different activist on 19 May, and an annual meeting on 26 May with no contested vote. The one genuine expectations gap that could work in the bull's favour is that the market may be underrating the operating recovery: the first quarter of 2026 showed attendance up 4%, spending per visitor up 6% to $69.26 and the seasonal loss narrowed by $48M, and management has openly targeted the gap between its 27% margin and regional peers above 30%. But the first quarter is the smallest quarter of the year, and July's weather damage lands in the third-quarter print reported in November. That gap will not be settled in this window.
valley_of_death: The next three to nine months are where this position is most exposed, and the exposure is already visible rather than hypothetical. The immediate event is second-quarter results on 6 August 2026. The second and third quarters are the entire year for a regional park operator, and the July news flow has been bad: on 19 July 2026 Citi cut its target from $24 to $19 citing hazardous air quality from Ontario wildfires affecting fourteen parks across the Upper Midwest and Great Lakes, with health advisories telling people to stay indoors during peak season; Guggenheim cut on the same theme. That damage falls into the third-quarter print reported in November, so there are two consecutive negative-skew events between now and the end of the year. Underneath sits the leverage. Net debt was $5.42B at 29 March 2026 against roughly $820M of expected annual earnings before interest, tax, depreciation and amortisation, or about six and a half times. The 2024 credit agreement carries a maximum net first-lien leverage covenant tested at the end of every quarter, so a bad season does not merely dent earnings - it compresses the headroom in a maintenance test. Interest expense runs near $95M a quarter. Free cash flow cannot help: capital spending absorbed about 93% of operating cash flow over the trailing twelve months, leaving roughly $29M of trailing free cash flow. The only real deleveraging lever is more asset sales, and each one sells earnings as well as debt. The mechanical risk to be explicit about: because the equity is only about a quarter of a $7.21B enterprise value, a disappointing season that takes the multiple from about nine times to about eight times is worth roughly $9 a share to the common - more than half the current price - without anything dramatic happening to the debt.
positioning_washout: The forced selling has mostly already happened, which is why the shares are near the bottom of a $12.51 to $31.99 range rather than in free fall. The old Cedar Fair was for decades an income vehicle with a substantial distribution, and its shareholder register was built accordingly. The dividend now stands at zero. That eviction of the yield-focused base is complete, not pending - it is the single biggest reason the shares de-rated from the low thirties. Similarly, the merger-arbitrage and merger-synergy holders who bought the 2024 Cedar Fair and Six Flags combination have had two years and a $1.19B goodwill write-off in the third quarter of 2025 to leave. What remains is a register split between event-driven money that bought the JANA story after October 2025 and value money underwriting the parks. The unfinished risk is on the event side: if the second-quarter print on 6 August 2026 is weak and the activist process visibly stalls into the 2027 nomination window, the event-driven holders have no reason to stay, and their exit is not disciplined by valuation. With a market value under $1.8B, that flow moves the price. There is also index risk - a company this size with negative book momentum can face mechanical selling on a downgrade out of mid-cap benchmarks. On the constructive side, a register that has already lost its income holders and taken its impairment is a cleaner starting point than one still shedding them. But 'the washout has happened' is a reason to look, not a reason to own - and it does not create a floor.
moderator_conclusion: Pass for now. This came to the committee described as a defined-risk special situation - risk about 6% to make about 76%, with the loss bounded by a floor at $16.50. Verification does not support either half of that. On the event: JANA Partners' demand that the board sell the company is real and still live, but it is undated, non-binding, and dependent on a buyer who has not appeared to finance an enterprise value above seven billion dollars. More importantly, the board has answered it without conceding it. Since the 17 March 2026 sale letter the company has installed an executive chairman (25 March 2026), signed a cooperation agreement with a different activist, H Partners, seating Rehan Jaffer (19 May 2026), held its annual meeting with no contested vote (26 May 2026), and filled out a turnaround management team with a new chief financial officer (17 June 2026) and chief operating officer (15 July 2026). Two of the three operating partners JANA originally named had already left the group by 24 November 2025 to pursue roles with the company. Boards that intend to sell hire bankers and announce reviews; this one hired operators. The proxy window that could have forced the question in 2026 has closed, and the next one is unannounced and roughly six to nine months away. On the floor, which matters more: there isn't one. The shares traded at $12.51 within the past twelve months, 29% below the level the write-up treats as protected. Behind that price sits $116.5M of cash against $5.53B of total debt, book equity of $279M, retained earnings of negative $2.03B after the $1.19B write-off in the third quarter of 2025, and trailing free cash flow of roughly $29M against interest expense near $380M a year. This is a levered equity stub in which the common is about a quarter of a $7.21B enterprise value, so one turn of multiple compression is worth roughly $9 to $10 a share. The only recent arm's-length transaction in these assets - EPR Properties paying $342M gross for seven parks - clears at roughly eight and a half times, below the ten and a half times the $31 target requires. Run the probabilities honestly and fair value lands at about $18 - a fifth of the outcomes around $30 on a sale, two fifths around $22 if the turnaround works, two fifths around $9 if attendance keeps sliding. That mean is within a dollar of the $17.59 market price. There is no edge in the valuation, and the near-term skew is negative: second-quarter results land 6 August 2026, July's wildfire-smoke attendance damage lands in the November print, Citi cut to $19 on 19 July and Guggenheim cut as well, and the quarterly net first-lien leverage covenant is tested through all of it. None of this says the business is worthless. The first quarter of 2026 was genuinely better - attendance up 4%, spending per visitor up 6% to $69.26, the seasonal loss narrowed by $48M - and the land under Cedar Point, Knott's Berry Farm and Magic Mountain cannot be replicated. If the new team closes the margin gap it has publicly acknowledged, this is a much better stock in two years. But that is a leveraged turnaround underwritten on execution, and it belongs in a different book with different sizing, not in an event sleeve where the whole justification is a bounded loss. What would change the answer: a formally announced strategic review or sale process; an identified bidder with committed financing; a JANA slate filed for the 2027 annual meeting; or the shares in the low teens after a capitulation print, where the reward-to-risk that was claimed at $17.59 would actually exist.
interrogator_dossier:
# FUN - Six Flags Entertainment Corporation

## Event-driven special situation: activist campaign for a sale of the company

**Interrogator dossier - forensic read of the EVENT, not the franchise.**
Prepared 28 July 2026. All prices and filings verified against live sources on that date.

---

## 0. WHAT THIS TRADE ACTUALLY IS

Six Flags Entertainment trades under the ticker FUN because the surviving legal entity of the
July 2024 merger is the old Cedar Fair vehicle. The company runs regional amusement parks
across North America - Cedar Point, Knott's Berry Farm, Magic Mountain, Great Adventure and
roughly forty others after recent disposals.

The reason this name reached our board is not the parks. It is JANA Partners, an activist
investment firm, which on 21 October 2025 disclosed an economic interest of about 9% alongside
the retired NFL player Travis Kelce, former Gap and Lululemon chief executive Glenn Murphy, and
technology executive Dave Habiger. On 17 March 2026 JANA sent the board a public letter
demanding it explore an outright sale of the company and remove the board chair. Our board
entry values a successful outcome at $31 a share against a supposed downside floor of $16.50,
implying reward-to-risk of about 2.6 to 1.

The core question for this dossier is narrow: is that event real, dated and binding, and is
that floor real? The answer to both is no.

---

## 1. NARRATIVE ARC - HOW THE EVENT HAS ACTUALLY DEVELOPED

The campaign has moved through four visible stages, and the direction of travel is away from a
sale, not toward one.

**Stage one - the stake (21 October 2025).** JANA discloses roughly 9% economic interest with a
celebrity-plus-operator group. The framing is collaborative: work with the board and management
to improve the guest experience and enhance value.

**Stage two - the group dissolves into the company (24 November 2025).** In its own release
applauding the hire of John Reilly as president and chief executive, JANA discloses that Glenn
Murphy "has de-grouped from the JANA-led investor group to advance discussions with Six Flags on
a potential senior leadership role with the Board," and that Dave Habiger "remains de-grouped
from the JANA-led investor group to enable him to pursue a complementary, but separate,
opportunity involving the Company." This is the language of a settlement, not a proxy fight. Two
of the three named operating partners left the activist group to take company roles within five
weeks of the stake being announced.

**Stage three - the escalation (17 March 2026).** With the shares still falling, JANA publicly
demands an immediate sale process and the ouster of the board chair, naming Murphy and Habiger
as prospective directors. This is the high-water mark of the campaign and the moment our board
entry was almost certainly seeded.

**Stage four - the board absorbs the pressure without selling (March to July 2026).** The
company's answer has been governance and asset sales, not a sale process:

| Date | Action | What it substitutes for |
|---|---|---|
| Nov 2025 / Dec 2025 | John Reilly appointed president and chief executive | New management instead of new owners |
| 4 March 2026 | Agreements to sell seven parks to EPR Properties, $331.4M cash ($342M gross) | Piecemeal asset sales instead of a whole-company sale |
| 25 March 2026 | Richard "Dick" Haddrill named executive chairman, effective immediately | Chair replacement conceded, sale not conceded |
| April 2026 | US portion of the EPR sale closes | Cash in, but only about 6% of net debt |
| 19 May 2026 | Cooperation agreement with H Partners; Rehan Jaffer joins the board after the annual meeting, replacing Arik Ruchim | A different activist is settled with a board seat |
| 26 May 2026 | 2026 annual meeting of stockholders held | The 2026 proxy window closes |
| 17 June 2026 | Ash Walia appointed chief financial officer | |
| 15 July 2026 | Mark Pauls appointed chief operating officer | |

Read the table as a whole and the pattern is unmistakable. Every demand JANA made has been
answered with something other than the thing it asked for. The chair was replaced - with a
turnaround executive chairman, not with a banker running a process. Board refreshment happened -
through a cooperation agreement with a *different* activist, H Partners. Assets were sold - seven
peripheral parks, not the company. And no sale process, strategic review, or data room has been
announced in any filing or release through 28 July 2026.

---

## 2. IS THE CATALYST REAL, DATED AND BINDING?

**Real: yes, partially.** JANA is a serious, well-resourced activist with a genuine 9% economic
interest and a public demand on the record. The campaign has not been withdrawn. That is more
than nothing.

**Dated: no.** There is no date attached to anything. Our own board entry carries the catalyst as
undated, and the verification confirms it. Worse, the one date that mattered has passed: the 2026
annual meeting was held on 26 May 2026. Director nominations for that meeting closed months
earlier, and no JANA slate went to a vote. The next natural forcing point - the nomination window
for the 2027 annual meeting - sits roughly six to nine months out and has no announced date.

**Binding: no.** Nothing here is contractual. A sale requires a third party to appear, agree a
price, and finance a transaction with an enterprise value above seven billion dollars against an
equity market value of under two billion. No bidder has been publicly identified. Reports of
"private equity interest" trace to commentary about the turnaround-heavy composition of the new
board, not to a disclosed approach.

The honest classification is a soft, non-binding, serially open-ended catalyst: real pressure,
no date, no contract, and a counterparty that does not yet exist.

---

## 3. THE FLOOR - THIS IS WHERE THE THESIS BREAKS

The board entry claims a downside floor of $16.50 against a live price of $17.59. That would mean
risking about 6% to make about 76%. It is not credible, and the tape has already falsified it.

**Falsification one - the stock has already traded 29% below the claimed floor.** The 52-week
range is $12.51 to $31.99. The claimed floor of $16.50 was breached within the last twelve months.
A level the security has recently traded straight through is not a floor.

**Falsification two - there is no asset backstop, because the debt eats it.** From the balance
sheet at 29 March 2026:

| Item | Amount |
|---|---|
| Cash and equivalents | $116.5M |
| Total debt (incl. finance leases) | $5.53B |
| Net debt | $5.42B |
| Minority interest | $235M |
| Total shareholders' equity | $279M |
| Enterprise value at $17.59 | ~$7.21B |
| Market capitalisation | ~$1.80B |

The equity is a thin slice - roughly a quarter of enterprise value - sitting on top of $5.4B of
net debt. That is the definition of a levered stub. Small changes in the multiple the market
applies to earnings swing the equity violently. Working the arithmetic on a full-year 2026
adjusted profit before interest, tax, depreciation and amortisation (adjusted EBITDA) of about
$820M, and using year-end net claims of roughly $5.4B including the minority interest:

| Multiple applied | Implied enterprise value | Implied value per share |
|---|---|---|
| 7.5x | $6.15B | ~$7 |
| 8.5x | $6.97B | ~$15 |
| 9.25x | $7.59B | ~$21 |
| 10.5x | $8.61B | ~$31 |

Two things fall out. First, the $31 target is not a mystery - it is simply a takeover multiple of
about 10.5 times. Second, and far more important, a single turn of multiple compression from
today takes the shares to roughly $7. There is no cash, no net asset value, and no unencumbered
collateral underneath this equity to stop that. The relevant market data point cuts the wrong
way: EPR Properties paid $342M gross for seven parks, a price consistent with roughly eight and a
half times their earnings - below, not above, where the whole company trades today.

**Falsification three - the earnings themselves are unstable.** Free cash flow is close to zero
once capital spending is taken out: capital expenditure absorbed about 93% of operating cash flow
over the trailing twelve months, leaving trailing free cash flow of roughly $29M against a $1.8B
market value. Interest expense runs about $95M a quarter, or close to $380M a year. The company
wrote off a very large amount of merger goodwill in the third quarter of 2025, posting a $1.19B
net loss (a loss of $11.80 a share) in that quarter alone. Shareholders' equity is down to $279M
and retained earnings stand at negative $2.03B.

The verified floor is not $16.50. On the evidence it is somewhere between $10 and $12 - the recent
low of $12.51 with no support beneath it - and in a genuine attendance recession it is
meaningfully lower. The trade as written on the board risks roughly 35% to make roughly 75%, not
6% to make 76%.

---

## 4. CREDIBILITY OF THE SPONSOR AND THE COUNTERPARTY

**JANA: credible as an investor, compromised as a forcing agent.** The firm has a long record and
a real position. But it let two of its three named operating partners de-group into company roles
within weeks, and it did not run a slate at the 2026 annual meeting. A separate activist, H
Partners, took the board seat that was available. An activist whose personnel end up inside the
company, and whose board seat goes to someone else, has been managed rather than obeyed.

**The board: credibly resistant.** Executive chairman Haddrill, a new chief executive, a new chief
financial officer and a new chief operating officer, all appointed within nine months, form a
management team assembled to fix the business, not to sell it. Boards that intend to sell hire
bankers and announce reviews. This one hired operators.

**Management on the numbers: early and mixed, but not evasive.** The first quarter of 2026 was
genuinely better - revenue up 12% to $225.6M, attendance up 4% to 2.9 million visits, spending
per visitor up 6% to $69.26, and the seasonal loss narrowed by $48M to a $123M adjusted EBITDA
loss. The first quarter is the smallest quarter of the year and carries little information. Mr
Reilly has been candid that the 27% margin the company earned in 2025 is not acceptable against
regional peers in the low thirties, which is honest, but he has not put a number or a date on the
improvement.

**The tape since has gone the other way.** On 19 July 2026 Citi cut its price target from $24 to
$19 with a neutral rating, and Guggenheim also cut on softer attendance, citing hazardous air
quality from Ontario wildfires affecting fourteen parks across the Upper Midwest and Great Lakes
during the peak season. Jefferies carries a below-consensus full-year 2026 adjusted EBITDA
estimate of about $865M and warns that street attendance and revenue assumptions are too high.

---

## 5. RED FLAGS

- **The claimed floor is not a floor.** The shares traded at $12.51 within the last year, 29%
  below the $16.50 the board entry treats as protected.
- **The proxy window for 2026 has closed.** The annual meeting was held 26 May 2026 without a
  contested vote. The nearest hard forcing point is the 2027 nomination window, unannounced.
- **The activist group has been partially absorbed.** Two of three named operating partners
  de-grouped in November 2025 to pursue roles with the company.
- **Leverage is the dominant variable.** Net debt of $5.42B against about $820M of expected
  annual earnings before interest, tax, depreciation and amortisation is roughly six and a half
  times. The credit agreement carries a maximum net first-lien leverage covenant tested every
  quarter, which limits how much room a bad season leaves.
- **No free cash flow to deleverage with.** Trailing free cash flow of roughly $29M cannot move a
  $5.4B debt load. Deleveraging depends entirely on further asset sales.
- **The dividend is gone.** The payout is zero, which for a business that spent decades as an
  income vehicle means the natural holder base has already been evicted.
- **Peak-season demand is deteriorating right now.** Two brokers cut targets in July on soft
  attendance, in the quarter that makes the year.
- **The asset-sale comparable prices the company below the target multiple.** EPR paid roughly
  eight and a half times for the seven-park package; the $31 target needs about ten and a half.

## 6. GREEN FLAGS

- The activist campaign is live and has not been withdrawn; the 9% economic interest remains
  disclosed.
- The board has visibly conceded on governance - a new executive chairman in March 2026 and a
  cooperation agreement seating H Partners' Rehan Jaffer in May 2026 - which is the pattern that
  sometimes precedes a sale by a year or more.
- The asset base has genuine local scarcity. Cedar Point, Knott's Berry Farm and Magic Mountain
  sit on land that cannot be replicated, which is why a financial buyer can underwrite a bid at
  all.
- Operating momentum in the first quarter of 2026 was real - attendance, pricing and spending per
  visitor all moved the right way, and the seasonal loss narrowed by $48M.
- The seven-park disposal closed and brought in $331.4M of cash, proving the board will sell
  assets under pressure.
- A management team built for a turnaround is now fully in place: chief executive from December
  2025, chief financial officer from 17 June 2026, chief operating officer from 15 July 2026.

---

## 7. HIDDEN SIGNALS

The most telling detail is the substitution pattern. Every time JANA asked for the company to be
sold, the company gave it something adjacent and cheaper: a chair, a director seat to a rival
activist, seven parks. That is a board that has read the leverage on its own balance sheet and
concluded that a forced sale at a depressed multiple hands the entire premium to the debt. With
net debt at roughly six and a half times earnings, a buyer at eight and a half times leaves
shareholders with a stub; a buyer at ten and a half times leaves them with $31. The board is
holding out for the second, and it can afford to wait far longer than a shareholder can.

The second signal is the H Partners agreement. When a company settles with the second activist
on the register while the first is publicly demanding a sale, it has found a way to look
responsive without doing the thing that was demanded. That is skilful defence, and it is bearish
for anyone underwriting a near-term sale.

---

## 8. CAPITAL-ALLOCATION VERDICT

**Trajectory: deteriorating.** Not because the business is collapsing - the first quarter
genuinely improved - but because the *event* has weakened at every step since March 2026. The
demand was made, the proxy window passed without a vote, the board answered with governance and
asset sales, and the shares have fallen from the low twenties toward the bottom of their range
while two brokers cut targets on soft peak-season attendance.

**The single thing the director must weigh:** this position is not the defined-risk special
situation the board entry describes. The catalyst is undated, non-binding and dependent on a
buyer who has not appeared, and the downside floor of $16.50 has already been broken by the
market within the past twelve months. Sizing it as a 6%-risk trade would be a serious error. It
is a levered equity stub in which one turn of multiple compression is worth roughly $10 a share.

**On the franchise, for completeness:** the moat is narrow and real - irreplaceable regional
land and local scarcity - but the evidence says it is eroding, with a 27% margin against peers
above 30%, a return on invested capital of about 4.4%, and attendance that needs weather and
consumer health to cooperate. The structural threat from competing experience spending is
manageable rather than terminal; this is a leverage and execution problem, not a melting
industry.

interrogator_dossier:
# Six Flags Entertainment (FUN) — Event Dossier

**Type:** Activist-driven special situation. The thesis is not the quality of the amusement-park business (it is a leveraged, cyclical, capital-hungry operator). The thesis is whether the activist campaign forces a sale or a real-estate monetization that closes the gap between today's roughly $20 share price and a mid-to-high-$20s to low-$30s value — with a downside floor in the mid-teens if nothing happens.

## 1. What the catalyst actually is

Six Flags is the merged Cedar Fair / Six Flags company (it kept Cedar Fair's old "FUN" ticker), North America's largest regional amusement-park operator. Since March 2026 it has been the target of an unusually public activist push:

- **JANA Partners** disclosed an economic interest of about 9% (a group that also includes former NFL player Travis Kelce and consumer executive Glenn Murphy). In a March 17, 2026 letter, JANA managing partner Scott Ostfeld called on the board to **replace its chair and engage with "known buyer interest" — i.e., explore an outright sale of the company.** The stock jumped nearly 20% on the stake's announcement.
- **Land & Buildings**, a real-estate-focused activist, has separately pushed Six Flags to **monetize its owned real estate** through a real-estate investment trust (REIT) spin-off or sale-leaseback — an approach it argued could deliver large upside on the theory that the parks sit on roughly $1B of underlying cash flow that the market values as an operating company rather than as real estate.
- **H Partners** reached a cooperation agreement on May 19, 2026 that put one of its people (Rehan Jaffer) on the board following the annual meeting.

So the "activist process" is real and multi-pronged. The problem is what has and has not happened since.

## 2. The forensic problem: the process is a push, not a signed event

The load-bearing question for a special situation is whether the catalyst is **dated and binding**. Here it is neither:

- **No sale process has been announced.** JANA is *asking* the company to run a sale and engage buyers. Management has not put itself up for sale, has not hired bankers for an auction, and there is no announced strategic review, no bidder, no signed deal, and therefore no deal price to arbitrage. This is a "convince management to sell" campaign, which can run for quarters or fizzle.
- **The proxy contest went the company's way.** At the May 26, 2026 annual meeting, **all three of the company's own director nominees were elected.** JANA did not win board seats through a contested vote. The only board change from an activist was the negotiated H Partners seat. That is a meaningful tell: shareholders did not hand the activists control, which weakens the near-term forcing pressure.
- **Management is running its own self-help playbook instead of a sale.** The company is executing the "Cedar-fication" turnaround (importing Cedar Fair's operating discipline into the legacy Six Flags parks), has been **selling parks and land to EPR Properties for about $331M** to cut debt, and has been reshuffling its own leadership — a new chief operating officer (Mark Pauls, effective July 15, 2026), a new chief financial officer (Ash Walia, May 2026), and other leadership transitions. This is management answering the activist with operational improvement and piecemeal asset sales, not by selling the whole company.

The net: the activist pressure has already delivered part of its value — cost cuts and asset sales the company might not otherwise have done, and a re-rating from the low-teens to around $20 — but the big prize (a full-company sale or a REIT conversion) is **undated, non-binding, and contested by a management team that is winning the governance fight.**

## 3. Downside floor — is it real?

The floor is a "no deal, turnaround muddles through" value, and it is reasonably well anchored:

- The stock's 52-week low is $12.51 and it has spent much of the past year building a base; the 200-day average sits near $18.70, just below today's $19.83. The low-teens is where the market valued the equity *before* the activist re-rate, so a full failure of the catalyst plausibly retraces toward the mid-teens.
- Jefferies' Street-low price target is $17 (January 2026). That is a credible "operating value, no premium" anchor.
- The floor is not bulletproof: this is a **levered** operator (net debt is large relative to a roughly $2B equity value), it is **economically cyclical** (consumer sentiment hit a record low in May 2026, which directly threatens discretionary theme-park spend), and its free cash flow is capital-intensive. A recession or a weak summer season could push the equity below the mid-teens, so the floor is "soft support," not contractual cash.

I anchor the verified floor at about **$16.50** — between the Jefferies $17 target and the pre-catalyst mid-teens base, haircut modestly for leverage and cyclicality.

## 4. Upside target — how derived

- Guggenheim's target is **$29** (cut from higher on the park sales). The recent analyst cluster (Jefferies/Truist/UBS) averages about $22, and the broader consensus is skewed by older, higher targets. A clean **sale** of the company would likely fetch a premium into the low $30s given private-equity and strategic interest in irreplaceable regional-park real estate; the Land & Buildings REIT case argues for even more, but that is the aggressive scenario, not the base.
- A reasonable **event-win target is about $31** — roughly a take-private premium or a successful real-estate monetization — consistent with the board dossier's target and with the top of the credible analyst range.

## 5. Red flags / green flags

🔴 **Undated and contested.** No banker, no auction, no deal, no proxy win for the activist. The single most important weakness.
🔴 **Cyclical demand into a weak-consumer tape.** Record-low consumer sentiment (May 2026) is a direct headwind to a discretionary business right before its key summer season.
🔴 **Leverage.** Piecemeal asset sales to EPR are partly *deleveraging out of necessity*, which can cap how much premium a buyer will pay for the equity.
🟢 **Real, engaged, credible activists** (JANA + Land & Buildings + an H Partners board seat) with a genuine sum-of-the-parts / real-estate angle, and management already delivering cost cuts and asset sales under the pressure.
🟢 **Live operational improvement:** Q1 2026 revenue up 12% to $225.6M, per-capita spending up 6%, roughly $33M of fixed-cost cuts — early evidence the self-help is working, which supports the floor even without a deal.
🟢 **Multiple ways to win:** whole-company sale, REIT conversion, or simply a continued operating re-rate.

## 6. Verdict for the director

This is a genuine activist special situation with a real floor and real engaged holders, but the catalyst is **a soft, non-binding, undated push to sell — not a hard, dated, contractual event.** The proxy vote went to management, and management is answering with self-help rather than a sale, so the forcing pressure is diffuse. Treat this as a mid-conviction, asymmetric-but-slow situation: you are paid to wait if the floor holds, but there is no scheduled date that forces the re-rating. The asymmetry (about $31 target versus about $16.50 floor from roughly $20) is attractive on paper, but the odds of the *win* leg firing on a defined timeline are only moderate.
